lesson_title: One Family, Same Speed: The Electromagnetic Spectrum
hook_text: Your radio, your remote, and the X-ray at the clinic are the same thing travelling at the same speed.
clip_script: Radio waves. Microwaves. Infrared. Light. Ultraviolet. X-rays. Gamma rays. Seven names, one family — and here is the part that surprises everybody: they all travel at exactly the same speed. Three hundred million metres every second. So what makes them different? Only how tightly packed they are. Long and lazy at one end, short and sharp at the other. And because the speed is stuck, they trade off perfectly — squeeze the waves shorter and more of them must arrive each second. That is the whole see-saw. Local FM sits around a hundred million waves a second, so each wave is about three metres — the length of a car aerial, and that is not a coincidence. A microwave oven runs at nearly two and a half billion a second, so its waves are only about twelve centimetres. Look at the mesh in the oven door: the holes are far smaller than that. The waves are too fat to get out. And the shorter they get, the harder each packet hits. Radio taps you like a feather. Ultraviolet flicks you — one packet carries about twelve million times the punch — and that is sunburn. X-rays go straight through you, which is why the radiographer hands you a lead apron and steps behind the screen.
visual_style: A single glowing wave stretched across the screen, compressing step by step from lazy radio ripples to a razor-tight gamma line, with everyday objects lighting up at each band — car aerial, oven door, remote, sunhat, lead apron.
pacing: Rapid seven-name opener, a slow beat on 'same speed', then accelerating compression to a hard stop on the lead apron.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and do c = fλ and E = hf without ever fumbling a prefix.
